plan.topic: Type 2 diabetes genetic risk vs lifestyle: low ultra-processed food intake plus 150 min/week of activity linked to about 49% lower risk in people at high genetic risk (EASD 2026 abstract, 56,964 UK Biobank adults, 926 cases over 7.8 years)
plan.angle: 'If diabetes runs in your family, is it written in your DNA?' Walk through what a polygenic risk score is, then the 3 findings: +7% risk per 10% rise in the UPF share of the diet, 39% lower risk when meeting the WHO activity guideline, and about 49% lower risk with both in the high-genetic-risk group. Explain what 'ultra-processed' means (NOVA) and why diet share isn't the same as calories. Add the practical, evidence-backed levers (guideline activity, swapping UPF staples) and link to established prevention evidence such as the Diabetes Prevention Program. Be clear on the limits: observational, a conference abstract not yet peer-reviewed, average age 69.5, mostly white UK participants, and 'linked to' not 'prevents'. Use 56,964 as the sample everywhere.

package.description:
Can you lower your diabetes risk if it runs in your family? A new 56,964-person study suggests your habits are still linked to your risk, even at high genetic risk.

QUICK ANSWER: In a 2026 study published in the journal Diabetes and presented at the EASD meeting, researchers followed 56,964 UK Biobank adults for about 7.8 years (926 new diabetes cases). People at high genetic risk who kept ultra-processed food low (about 11% or less of their food by weight) AND met the WHO's 150-minutes-a-week activity guideline, measured by a wrist tracker, had about 49% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes. That's a relative figure: overall, about 1.6% of participants developed diabetes. Participants averaged 69.5 years old, and the genetic analysis included only people of European ancestry, so results may differ for other groups. It's peer-reviewed but observational, so it shows a link, not proof — but it points the same way as the randomized Diabetes Prevention Program trial, where an intensive lifestyle program led to 58% fewer new diabetes cases than placebo over about 2.8 years in 3,234 adults who already had raised blood sugar.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
• What a polygenic risk score actually measures — and why "high risk" isn't destiny
• How every 10% rise in the ultra-processed share of the diet (by weight) was linked to about 7% higher diabetes risk
• How meeting the WHO's 150-minutes-a-week activity guideline, measured by wrist tracker, was linked to about 39% lower risk
• What "ultra-processed" means under the NOVA food classification system
• How the randomized Diabetes Prevention Program trial (3,234 adults with raised blood sugar) cut new diabetes cases by 58% over about 2.8 years, and what was still true 15 years later (27% lower incidence)
• Four simple, evidence-based steps if diabetes runs in your family

This video is for general education only and isn't medical advice. If diabetes runs in your family or you've been told you have prediabetes, talk to your clinician about testing. If you take medication, don't change anything without speaking to your clinician first.

Sources: Xu W et al., Diabetes (2026), https://doi.org/10.2337/db26-0395 · NHGRI, Polygenic Risk Scores · CDC, Diabetes Risk Factors · CDC, Prediabetes · Florez JC et al., NEJM (2006) · CDC, A U.S. Report Card

script.working_title: Diabetes Runs in Your Family? What a 57,000-Person Study Says You Can Still Change
script.target_keyword: can you prevent diabetes if it runs in family
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim + open loop: a 56,964-person analysis challenges "it's in your genes", and the payoff (a 1990s trial and what happened to its volunteers 15 years later) is held back until late in the video

scenes.narration: If type 2 diabetes runs in your family, you've probably been told it's in your genes. Like a countdown clock you can't switch off.
scenes.retention_device: Visceral 'you' scenario that names the viewer's fear

scenes.narration: But a new analysis of 56,964 adults suggests your genes may not get the final say.

visual.stat_label: UK Biobank adults in the analysis

scenes.retention_device: Counterintuitive claim with a concrete number

scenes.narration: Among people at the highest genetic risk, two everyday habits together were linked to about 49% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

visual.stat_label: Linked lower risk, high-genetic-risk group, observational

scenes.retention_device: Big surprising stat as proof point

scenes.narration: In the next few minutes, you'll learn what a genetic risk score actually measures, what really counts as ultra-processed food, and three of the study's key findings in plain numbers.

items: What a genetic risk score means

scenes.retention_device: Clear promise of what the viewer gets

scenes.narration: And stay to the end. A trial that began in the 1990s already put this idea to a real test, and what happened to its volunteers years later is the part most people never hear.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, paid off in 'The trial that tested it'

scenes.narration: So first: what do your genes actually do here?
The family part is real. The CDC lists having a parent, brother or sister with type 2 diabetes as a risk factor.
scenes.retention_device: Validates the viewer before challenging the belief

scenes.narration: But there's no single 'diabetes gene'. A 2024 study of more than 2.5 million people mapped 611 regions of the genome linked to type 2 diabetes.

visual.stat_label: Genome regions linked to type 2 diabetes

scenes.retention_device: Surprising number that breaks the 'one gene' myth

scenes.narration: Each one nudges risk by a tiny amount. So scientists add them up into a polygenic risk score. Think of it as a genetic weather forecast, not a verdict.
A high score means higher odds on average. But according to the US National Human Genome Research Institute, it can't tell you whether you personally will get the disease.

visual.myth: A high genetic score means you'll get diabetes
visual.fact: It estimates odds across a population, not your fate

scenes.narration: And a forecast of rain doesn't stop you from grabbing an umbrella. The real question is: does the umbrella work?
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before the section change

scenes.narration: This new study offers some clues.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card that picks up the question with a new setup

scenes.narration: The data comes from UK Biobank, a huge research project that has followed about half a million British adults for years.

visual.stock_query: map of UK with people icons

scenes.narration: Researchers analyzed 56,964 of them, with an average age of 69.5, and tracked who developed type 2 diabetes over about 7.8 years.
926 people did. That's about one in 60. Keep that number in your pocket, because it matters later.

visual.stat_label: New type 2 diabetes cases over 7.8 years

scenes.retention_device: Mini open loop, paid off in finding 3

scenes.narration: They looked at two things people can change: how much of the diet, by weight, was ultra-processed food, and whether a wrist tracker showed people meeting the World Health Organization's guideline of 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a week.

items: Ultra-processed share of diet, by weight
visual.stock_query: plate and wrist tracker side by side

scenes.narration: One note up front. This study was just published in the journal Diabetes and is being presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes meeting. It's peer-reviewed, but it's observational. We'll come back to why that matters.
scenes.retention_device: Transparency plus a promised return, paid off in 'The fine print'

scenes.narration: Finding number one is about what's on your plate.
For every 10% rise in the share of the diet, by weight, that was ultra-processed, the risk of type 2 diabetes was about 7% higher.

visual.stat_label: Risk per 10% rise in UPF share, by weight

scenes.narration: But what does 'ultra-processed' actually mean? It's not just 'food made in a factory'.
Most researchers use the NOVA system, which sorts food into four groups.
Frozen peas and plain oats are minimally processed. Olive oil and butter are culinary ingredients. Canned fish and simple cheeses count as processed.

Ultra-processed foods are industrial formulations, usually made with ingredients you'd rarely find in a home kitchen, like protein isolates, high-fructose corn syrup, hydrogenated oils, flavorings and emulsifiers.
Think soft drinks, packaged snacks, many breakfast cereals, instant noodles and reconstituted meat products.
Now, a common mix-up. A higher share of ultra-processed food isn't the same thing as eating more calories.

visual.myth: A higher ultra-processed share means eating more calories
visual.fact: Share describes what your diet is made of
visual.stock_query: pie chart plate versus calorie counter

scenes.narration: Two people can eat exactly the same number of calories. For one, most of the plate is ultra-processed. For the other, very little is. Same total, very different plate.

visual.stock_query: two plates same size different food

scenes.narration: So this finding is about the make-up of the diet, not simply eating too much. But one clever experiment showed the two can be connected.
scenes.retention_device: 'But here's where it gets interesting' pivot into a micro-story

scenes.narration: In 2019, scientists at the US National Institutes of Health had 20 adults live on a research ward for four weeks.
scenes.retention_device: Micro-story about an unusual study design

scenes.narration: For two weeks they got ultra-processed meals, and for two weeks, unprocessed meals. The meals offered were matched for calories, sugar, fat, fiber and salt, and people could eat as much as they wanted.

visual.stock_query: two meal trays side by side

scenes.narration: On the ultra-processed diet, people ate about 500 more calories a day and gained about 0.9 kilograms in two weeks.

visual.stat_label: Calories eaten per day, ultra-processed diet

scenes.narration: That was a small, short study. It measured eating and body weight, not diabetes. But it hints at one way ultra-processed diets might push risk upward.

And the bigger picture fits. A 2024 umbrella review in The BMJ, covering studies with almost 10 million participants, rated the dose-response link between ultra-processed food and type 2 diabetes as 'convincing', still based on observational studies.

visual.attribution: BMJ umbrella review 2024, dose-response link with type 2 diabetes, observational studies

scenes.retention_device: Zoom out to stronger evidence before the section change

scenes.narration: Finding number two is about something you do with your legs, not your fork.
People whose wrist tracker showed they met the WHO activity guideline had about 39% lower risk of type 2 diabetes than those who didn't.

visual.stat_label: Linked lower risk, tracker-measured WHO guideline met
visual.stock_query: person with wrist tracker walking briskly

scenes.narration: The WHO guideline for adults is at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix of both.
150 minutes sounds like a lot. It's 30 minutes, five days a week. Or about 21 minutes a day.

visual.stat_label: Per day adds up to 150 a week

scenes.retention_device: Reframes the number to feel doable

scenes.narration: Moderate means your breathing picks up but you can still talk. Brisk walking counts. So do cycling and dancing.
Why would muscles matter for blood sugar? Working muscles pull glucose out of your blood to use as fuel.
And regular activity can help your body respond better to insulin, the hormone that moves sugar into your cells.
But so far we've looked at diet and activity one at a time. So what happened in people with the worst genetic odds who had both?

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: Finding number three is the one that speaks most directly to family history.

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: Researchers grouped people by their polygenic risk score, from lower to higher genetic risk.

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: In the high-genetic-risk group, people who both kept ultra-processed food low, about 11% or less of their food by weight, and met the activity guideline had about 49% lower risk of type 2 diabetes.

visual.stat_label: Both habits, high genetic risk, observational

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: Roughly half. In the group that had drawn the toughest genetic hand.
scenes.retention_device: Emotional beat with a short sentence

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: Now, remember the number I asked you to keep in your pocket? About one in 60.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the earlier mini loop

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: A 49% lower risk is a relative drop. It doesn't mean 49 percentage points come off your personal odds.

visual.myth: 49% lower risk means 49 points off your odds
visual.fact: It's a relative drop compared with a starting risk

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: Overall, about 1.6% of people in this study developed type 2 diabetes during follow-up. How much any one person's odds would change depends on where they start, and the headline number doesn't show that.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising reframe with the absolute number

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: That doesn't make the finding trivial. Prediabetes is extremely common, so across millions of people, a lower relative risk could add up to a lot of cases, if it holds up.

visual.stock_query: city of people with small icons

scenes.section: Finding 3: Both, at high genetic risk
scenes.narration: And that's a big 'if'. Here's the fine print most headlines will skip.
Four limits you need to know before you believe any headline about this study.
Here they are.
First, it's observational. It shows a link, not proof that eating less ultra-processed food or exercising caused the lower risk.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the earlier 'we'll come back to why that matters'

scenes.narration: People who move more and eat less ultra-processed food may differ in other ways too, like income, smoking or weight. Researchers try to adjust for those factors, but they can't catch everything.

Second, diet was self-reported. People recalled what they ate over 24 hours, and sorting those foods into ultra-processed or not isn't always precise. Activity was measured better, with a wrist tracker worn for a week.

visual.stock_query: person recalling meals with thought bubble

scenes.narration: Third and fourth: the average participant was 69.5, and the genetic analysis only included people of European ancestry. Results might differ for younger people, or for groups with higher risk, such as people of South Asian, Chinese, Black African or Black Caribbean background.
scenes.retention_device: Speaks directly to viewers outside the sample

scenes.narration: UK Biobank volunteers also tend to be healthier than the general population, which can shape the results.
So it's 'linked to', not 'prevents'. Which raises the obvious question: has anyone actually tested whether changing habits prevents diabetes?

visual.myth: This study proves habits prevent diabetes
visual.fact: It shows a link; trials test prevention

scenes.retention_device: Question that reopens the main loop

scenes.narration: Yes. And this is the trial I promised you at the start.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: In the Diabetes Prevention Program, US researchers enrolled 3,234 adults with raised blood sugar who didn't yet have diabetes.

visual.stat_label: Adults with raised blood sugar enrolled

scenes.narration: One group got an intensive lifestyle program. The goals were to lose at least 7% of body weight and do at least 150 minutes of physical activity a week.

items: Lose at least 7% of body weight

scenes.narration: Over an average of about 2.8 years, the lifestyle group had 58% fewer new cases of diabetes than the placebo group.

visual.stat_label: Diabetes incidence vs placebo, about 2.8 years

scenes.narration: A Finnish trial of 522 people published the year before found the same figure: 58% lower.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising coincidence that strengthens the case

scenes.narration: Now, the part most people never hear. Researchers kept following the Diabetes Prevention Program volunteers, and after 15 years, the lifestyle group still had 27% lower diabetes incidence than the placebo group.

visual.stat_label: Diabetes incidence vs placebo after 15 years

scenes.narration: The benefit shrank over time, but it didn't disappear.

And genes? In a follow-up analysis of the same trial, people carrying high-risk versions of a well-known diabetes gene called TCF7L2 still appeared to benefit from the lifestyle program, though that analysis was too small to be certain.
scenes.on_screen_text: High-risk gene, still appeared to benefit
scenes.retention_device: Links the trial back to the genetics question

scenes.narration: These trials didn't test ultra-processed food specifically, and they studied people who already had raised blood sugar. But they were randomized, which is stronger evidence, and they point the same way as the new study.
So if diabetes runs in your family, here's what the evidence supports. None of it needs a genetic test.
One: know your numbers. The CDC estimates about 115 million American adults, more than 2 in 5, have prediabetes, and 8 in 10 of them don't know it.

visual.stat_label: US adults with prediabetes, CDC estimate

scenes.narration: With a family history, ask your clinician whether a blood sugar test, like an HbA1c or a fasting glucose, makes sense for you.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask about a blood sugar test

scenes.narration: Two: build toward the WHO guideline, 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, in whatever chunks fit your life. The WHO is clear that some activity is better than none.
Three: shift the share, not just the calories. Swap one ultra-processed staple at a time.
For example, sugary cereal for plain oats with fruit. Soft drinks for water or sparkling water. Packaged snacks for fruit or plain nuts. A few instant meals for simple home-cooked ones.

items: Soft drink → water or sparkling water
Packaged snacks → fruit or plain nuts

scenes.narration: These aren't magic foods. They just move your diet from NOVA group four back toward group one.

Four: if you've been told you have prediabetes, ask about a structured program. In the US, the CDC's National Diabetes Prevention Program offers a year-long lifestyle change program. In England, the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme offers something similar.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to the trial that tested it

scenes.narration: And if you already take medication, don't change anything on your own. Talk it through with your clinician first.

So, is diabetes written in your DNA? Your genes may set your starting odds. But in this study of 56,964 adults, even at the highest genetic risk, how people ate and moved was linked to very different outcomes.
It's not proof yet. But it lines up with decades of trial evidence, and every lever in this video is something you can start this week.
Next, we're breaking down which everyday foods are ultra-processed, including a few 'healthy' ones that surprise people. Subscribe to InforMed so you catch it.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the core numbers and they are accurate. The new study (Xu W et al., Diabetes 2026, DOI 10.2337/db26-0395) matches the Medical Xpress and Science Media Centre (SMC) coverage: 56,964 adults, average age 69.5, 7.8 years of follow-up, 926 cases, +7% risk per 10% ultra-processed share by weight, −39% for meeting the activity guideline, −49% for both habits in the high-genetic-risk group, and a low-intake cut-off of ≤11%. It used 24-hour recalls, a wrist tracker worn for a week, and genetic data from people of European ancestry only. The supporting sources also check out: the 2019 NIH inpatient trial (20 adults, ~500 kcal/day, 0.9 kg), the 2024 Nature genetics study (611 regions, >2.5M people), the Diabetes Prevention Program (3,234 people, 2.8 years, −58%), the Finnish trial (522 people, NEJM 2001, −58%), the 15-year DPP follow-up (−27%), the TCF7L2 gene analysis (difference between groups not statistically significant, so the hedged wording is right), and the CDC figures (115.2M adults, >2 in 5, 8 in 10 unaware; report dated 16 March 2026).

The framing is careful: it separates relative from absolute risk, calls the study observational, gives the absolute rate and lists the limits. It includes a medication caveat and tells viewers to see a clinician about testing.

One major problem: the script leaves out a limitation that two independent experts raised in the SMC reaction. When ultra-processed food was split into subgroups, only ultra-processed drinks stayed significantly linked to diabetes after full adjustment. Without that, Finding 1 and the 'shift the share' advice overstate what the study says about ultra-processed food as a whole. The other items are minor wording fixes.

issues.location: s19 / s31-s32 / s54 (Finding 1 and fine print)
issues.claim: For every 10% rise in the share of the diet, by weight, that was ultra-processed, the risk of type 2 diabetes was about 7% higher.
issues.problem: This leaves out a key limitation from independent experts (Prof Alberto Fiore and Seamus Higgins, quoted in the SMC reaction [S1a]). When ultra-processed food was broken into subgroups, only ultra-processed drinks stayed significantly linked to diabetes after full adjustment. The experts say this points to sugary drinks rather than processing itself. Without it, viewers are led to believe all ultra-processed foods were shown to carry the risk.
issues.fix: Add a new scene after s31 (source_ids S1, S1a). Narration: "One more detail. When researchers split ultra-processed foods into types, only ultra-processed drinks stayed clearly linked to diabetes after full adjustment. Independent experts say that points to sugary drinks, not processing itself, doing much of the work." On-screen text: "Drinks drove the link". Also change s54 narration to: "Second, diet was self-reported. People recalled what they ate over 24 hours, and that method wasn't designed to measure ultra-processed food, so foods can be misclassified. Activity was measured better, with a wrist tracker worn for a week."

issues.claim: Three: shift the share, not just the calories. Swap one ultra-processed staple at a time.
issues.problem: Once the drinks finding is disclosed, the advice should put the swap with the strongest evidence first.
issues.fix: s71 narration: "Three: shift the share, not just the calories. Swap one ultra-processed staple at a time, and in this study, sugary drinks are the clearest place to start." In s72, move 'Soft drink → water or sparkling water' to the top of the list.

issues.claim: Among people at the highest genetic risk, two everyday habits together were linked to about 49% lower risk
issues.problem: The study's group is 'high genetic risk' (s43 says so too). 'Highest' is stronger and doesn't match.
issues.fix: Narration: "Among people at high genetic risk, two everyday habits together were linked to about 49% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes."

issues.claim: In 2019, scientists at the US National Institutes of Health had 20 adults live on a research ward for four weeks.
issues.problem: The trial was published in 2019 but carried out in 2018.
issues.fix: Narration: "In a study published in 2019, scientists at the US National Institutes of Health had 20 adults live on a research ward for four weeks."

issues.claim: according to the US National Human Genome Research Institute, it can't tell you whether you personally will get the disease.

hold_reason: Dropped by Editor-in-Chief: Two major problems are unfixed. The script leaves out the expert-flagged limitation that only ultra-processed drinks stayed significantly linked to type 2 diabetes, so the ultra-processed food finding and the swap advice overstate the study. The YouTube description is cut off mid-word, with no medical disclaimer, no clinician/medication line and no sources.

notes: The shield mascot's speech bubble 'Habits still matter!' sits directly on top of the '-49%' number, and the sub-line 'Linked lower risk...' overlaps the DNA icon and the 'High genetic risk' pill underneath it — both the stat and the caption are hard to read.

At the 21.3s frame the 'Low ultra-processed diet' and '150 min activity' labels overlap each other directly (confirmed by layout audit), making both unreadable; a later frame in the same shot fixes the spacing, so the collision is only transient but still visible on screen.
At 37.7s a red question-mark decoration overlaps the word 'million' in the headline stat, partially covering the 'm', which hurts the one-second readability of the big number.

At 55.0s the headline 'Easy swaps' sits directly over the mascot cell's face, covering its eyes — the character reads as broken/covered rather than cute, and the frame is otherwise nearly empty gradient background.

In both frames ('Easy swaps' and 'Ask about a prevention program') the headline text overlaps the mascot's face/eyes, and the supporting molecule icons are tiny and scattered, leaving the frame feeling empty.
The 69.5s frame repeats the same headline-over-mascot-face overlap as shots 9/10; the 73.5s room-scene frame is clean and readable.
Headline 'Genes set odds, not outcomes' sits on top of the mascot's face in both sampled frames, obscuring the character; molecule elements are tiny specks that don't add visual interest.
'Next: surprising UPF foods' headline again overlaps the mascot's eyes/face in both frames; background feels sparse aside from a few tiny yellow molecule dots.

The 99.0s frame is clean and well-composed, but the 103.5s frame shows three stacked blue cell icons with an accompanying number caption rendered far too small (~24px per the layout audit) beneath them, effectively unreadable at a glance.

At 115.6s the headline 'What genes actually do' overlaps the mascot/DNA artwork underneath it, and the speech bubble 'Who am I really?' also crosses into the headline text, creating a cluttered pile of overlapping elements with no single clear focal point.
DNA mascot with 'Genome' label and speech bubble sits small in the left half of frame; the entire right half is empty purple background — no headline or supporting graphic to anchor the beat
Single small DNA icon floats alone on a mostly empty purple gradient with no label, title or supporting graphic — reads as a dead transition frame
DNA icon and the 'Risk forecast' weather icon sit far apart on opposite sides of the frame with a large dead gap between them, so the two ideas don't visually connect
DNA icon and the small blue cell circle are isolated on opposite sides of the frame with empty space between — same disconnected-icon composition as the previous shot

audio.soundNotes: Levels were already well auto-tuned: most cues sit around −14 to −16 dB under the voice (right in target) and music under speech (−14.5 dB) / in pauses (−14.7 dB) are both on-target, so I only nudged music up slightly (×1.15) for more felt presence in pauses and big reveals. I thinned a handful of redundant blips/pops in dense list-reveal clusters (chips/examples) to keep each second under the 3–4 effect ceiling, and tried to rescue a few near-silent swell cues (likely ducking artifacts) by maxing their gain, though a couple may still be inaudible given the linear gain cap. Added 5 bespoke atmospheric SFX (heartbeat accents on genetic-risk and closing lines, hospital-ward murmur for the NIH shot, a clipboard clack for the trial reveal, and a sizzling-pan cue for the food-swap section) to add texture the stock kit can't cover.
